title: Russia gives Indonesia no third pole at sea
gist: Radityo Dharmaputra argues Russia cannot serve as a 'third pole' for Indonesia against China, since Moscow is trade-dependent on Beijing and has endorsed China's bilateral formula for South China Sea disputes. The Tuna gas block, half-owned by sanctioned Zarubezhneft, shows Russian ownership gave no protection in the 2021 Chinese stand-off and now adds sanctions risk that has blocked an FID.

themes.theme: Russia cannot balance China for Jakarta

insights.claim: Russia cannot be a 'third pole' in Indonesia's bebas-aktif foreign policy to offset China, because Russia depends on China and has accepted Beijing's procedure for the South China Sea.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Indonesian hedging via Moscow does not reduce China exposure for Indonesian assets.
insights.quote: this third pole has no grounds, because Russia depends on China itself and has accepted Beijing’s procedure for the South China Sea

insights.claim: Per a Carnegie Endowment estimate, Beijing accounts for over 30% of Russia's export revenues and over 40% of its imports, while Russia was just 3% of China's exports and 5% of imports in 2024.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Asymmetric dependence means Moscow will not cross Beijing on third-party issues.
insights.quote: “Beijing accounts for more than 30% of Russia’s export revenues and provides over 40% of its imports”

insights.claim: The 4 February 2022 Russia-China joint statement told third states in advance that their cooperation would not be affected by third countries' choices.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Third countries cannot leverage Russia against China.

insights.claim: Putin and Xi signed a 20 May 2026 joint statement backing resolution of the South China Sea dispute through talks among directly involved states and opposing outside interference, a formula China reused in July.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Russia is aligned with China's bilateral approach, weakening claimant states' leverage.

insights.claim: Russian state oil firm Zarubezhneft acquired half of the Tuna gas block off the Natuna Islands in 2020, in waters China claims under its nine-dash line.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Tuna block sits in contested waters with dual geopolitical risk.

insights.claim: When a rig arrived at Tuna on 30 June 2021, a Chinese coast guard vessel appeared within days and Chinese diplomats demanded Indonesia stop drilling, despite the block being half Russian-owned.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Russian equity provided no deterrence against Chinese pressure on the project.

insights.claim: Jakarta refused China's demand and kept the rig working until 19 November 2021, with Harbour Energy as operator completing exploration.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Indonesia has precedent of resisting Chinese pressure on Natuna energy.

insights.claim: In May 2026 Harbour Energy sold its half of Tuna to Indonesia's Prime Group, and Zarubezhneft said it was ready to resume work in June.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Ownership change at Tuna shifts project risk onto Prime Group and the Russian partner.

insights.claim: Sanctions on Zarubezhneft after 2022 made financing difficult and kept Tuna partners from a final investment decision, per Bloomberg Technoz in October 2025.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Tuna FID remains unlikely while a sanctioned partner holds half.

insights.claim: The British government added Zarubezhneft to its sanctions list on 8 October as a Russian government-affiliated entity.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: UK listing can cut the project off from finance and insurance markets.

insights.claim: A Russian partner at Tuna adds sanctions risk while providing Jakarta no protection against China.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Negative risk-reward for Russian participation in Indonesian upstream.
insights.quote: A Russian partner at Tuna adds sanctions risk and gives Jakarta no protection against China.

insights.claim: Before committing further, Jakarta should check whether the UK listing cuts Tuna off from finance and insurance and whether Zarubezhneft's nominated oil suppliers pass sanctions screening.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Key diligence checkpoints for any Tuna-linked financing or insurance exposure.

themes.theme: Beijing's calculus and Jakarta's own concessions

insights.claim: The 2021 stand-off contradicts a view that Beijing would not risk its alignment with Moscow to disrupt a single offshore energy project; any Chinese restraint now may instead reflect its preoccupation with the Philippines.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Chinese forbearance at Natuna is contingent and could reverse if Philippine tensions ease.

insights.claim: Prabowo's November 2024 joint statement with Xi recorded a 'common understanding on joint development in areas of overlapping claims', weakening Jakarta's position in the North Natuna Sea despite later foreign-ministry denials.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Ambiguity on joint development raises legal risk for Natuna upstream projects.

insights.claim: The new foreign minister's first Commission I hearing is the place to state on record that the 2024 joint statement does not cover Tuna.
insights.speaker: Radityo Dharmaputra
insights.so_what: Watch the hearing for clarity on Tuna's legal status.
